messages.author: 2534b4a2ba9ce6a1
messages.subject: Line length in complex topography
parts:
Since density estimates typically refer to unit area as measured on a 2-D
map, I was wondering how to most appropriately determine individual transect
line length and total line length in topographically diverse habitats.

A) Should transects be x units long, as plotted on a map (e.g., with a
GIS), even though the distance actually walked may be >x units after going
up and down hills, ridges, etc. to get from one endpoint to the next?

or

B) Should transect length be measured along the ground, while going up
and down hills, ridges, etc. until you reach x units?

Intuitively, since inferences are 2 dimensional, A seems to me to be the
correct choice. However, if some parts of the study area are more complex
than others, the actual distance walked will be greater on some transects of
the same mapped length and more animals may be counted on those transects.
Does this pose any practical or theoretical problems?

I apologize if I missed this in the book.

messages.author: 98edb56c9e42fc5b
messages.subject: Re: Line length in complex topography
parts:
> >A) Should transects be x units long, as plotted on a map (e.g., with a
> >GIS), even though the distance actually walked may be >x units after going
> >up and down hills, ridges, etc. to get from one endpoint to the next?
> >
> > or
> >
> >B) Should transect length be measured along the ground, while going up
> >and down hills, ridges, etc. until you reach x units?

Seems to me that B would be the more accurate method. Suppose you
were going to measure wildlife along a river corridor.

Consider if you drew your 2-D line plotted over a river, in a
straight line, as if lying on your side. This would be at right
angles to that which you might plot over a 3-D up and down of
terrain, and the bends of the river could be envisioned as the up and
down of the undulating "terrain" of the river. Your line would be
"straight", as in the line of a dollar sign -> $.

You would miss all wildlife at the bends in the river, or worse
measure in many instances only the wildlife in upland areas between
straight stretches of the river... You would, in short, count things
on a straight line, but you would or could miss quite a lot of the
river!

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Line length in complex topography
parts:
> > Since density estimates typically refer to unit area as measured on a 2-D
> > map, I was wondering how to most appropriately determine individual transect
> > line length and total line length in topographically diverse habitats.
> >

> > A) Should transects be x units long, as plotted on a map (e.g., with a
> > GIS), even though the distance actually walked may be >x units after going
> > up and down hills, ridges, etc. to get from one endpoint to the next?
> >
> > or
> >
> > B) Should transect length be measured along the ground, while going up
> > and down hills, ridges, etc. until you reach x units?
> >

> > Intuitively, since inferences are 2 dimensional, A seems to me to be the
> > correct choice. However, if some parts of the study area are more complex
> > than others, the actual distance walked will be greater on some transects of
> > the same mapped length and more animals may be counted on those transects.
> > Does this pose any practical or theoretical problems?
> >
> > I apologize if I missed this in the book.

You didn't ... perhaps this is something we should include in the next
edition. You're right - A is correct. We have to work with 2D
projections simply because the surface area is a function of the scale you
measure it at ... the finer the scale, the greater the surface area. This
is related to measuring the length of a coastline ... which gets
progressively longer as your data get more precise.

So densities on steep slopes have the potential to be greater simply
because there is more habitat available per flat km^2.

Steve Buckland
